# Module X86 — x86-64

For code that runs on x86-64. What the standard's requirements mean on this machine and the machine's own rules, with
the reasons. A binding that names this module says which baseline level it builds for (X86.1), which cores it measures
on (X86.11) and which of these rules it checks; the rest is advice. Prices below come from named sources on named
cores and were read in September 2026; they differ between vendors and move with microcode, so a price here is the
prior and a measurement (10.8) is the fact.

## The machine

An x86-64 core in 2026 is a wide out-of-order engine behind a variable-length instruction set. Four facts drive the
rest.

- **Instructions are a compression format for µops.** Decode is the narrow point, so hot loops must run from the
  decoded-µop cache; Zen 5 decodes four instructions per clock for one thread and holds 6K µops in its op cache
  [Fog §25.2–25.4]. Register moves and zero idioms are resolved at rename and cost nothing [Fog §25.13].
- **Latency chains set the speed, not instruction counts.** A window of several hundred µops finds parallelism only
  where the code has it. Fog lists every Zen 5 vector instruction at an effective latency of 2 clocks, because the
  scheduler is nearly always full when latency counts [Fog §25.9]; a loop with one accumulator runs at that latency.
- **Memory is the long tail of the price list**, and its granularity leaks into correctness: 64-byte lines, 4 KiB
  pages, and a locked operation that spans two lines is a split lock that stalls every core [SDM3 §10.1].
- **The memory model is TSO, not sequential consistency.** The one visible reordering is a load completing before an
  older store to another address. x86-TSO is the formal model, checked against hardware after the vendors' prose proved
  ambiguous [TSO p.2] [SDM3 §10.2]; it is what the code is written against.

And it is not one machine. `pdep` is one µop on Intel and on Zen 3 onward and is microcoded at about 18 cycles on Zen 2
[uops-PDEP]; 64-bit `div` fell from tens of cycles on Skylake to 14 on Ice Lake [uops-DIV]; a microcode update removed
a store-elimination fast path from shipping Ice Lake parts [Downs-zero]. The expert reasons from a model and confirms on
each target [Downs-limits].

## Requirements

**X86.1 Baseline named, everything above it dispatched.** Code shall name the microarchitecture level it is built for
(`x86-64-v2`, `-v3` or `-v4`, as the psABI defines them [psABI L39–81]) and dispatch above it at run time. A dispatcher
shall check that the operating system saves the register state (`XGETBV`) as well as that the CPU has the feature
(`CPUID`), as BLAKE3 does before enabling AVX-512 [B3-dispatch L108–165]. New server code assumes v3, which RHEL 10
requires [RHEL10]; AVX-512 is present on Intel servers and on AMD from Zen 4 and absent from Intel clients since Alder
Lake, so it is always dispatched, never assumed.
> *Means* — 4.5, 10.8 [psABI]. *Governs* — effect. *CALM* — not applicable. *Checked by* — the build's `-march`
> recorded in the binding; a test run on the oldest supported core. *Brief* — Name the baseline level; dispatch above
> it; a dispatcher checks XGETBV as well as CPUID.

**X86.2 The chain, not the count.** A hot loop shall be written against its loop-carried dependency chain: enough
independent accumulators, streams or lanes to cover latency × throughput (eight for FMA on Zen 5, at 4 cycles and two
per clock [Fog §25.9]); memory operands and addressing modes that stay fused; zero idioms and register moves that the
renamer removes [Fog §25.13]. The bottleneck the code is expected to hit is written down before it is measured (X86.11).
The same principle at scale: zstd's Huffman decoder keeps four bit-streams in flight [Zstd-huf], and BLAKE3 hashes
eight or sixteen chunks at once, one per lane.
> *Means* — 10.8 [Downs-limits] [Fog]. *Governs* — transformation. *CALM* — not applicable. *Checked by* — the
> bottleneck named with the measurement (10.8). *Brief* — Write hot loops against the carried chain: accumulators
> ≥ latency × throughput; fused operands; zero idioms.

**X86.3 Branchless only where unpredictable.** A `cmov`, `setcc` or mask shall replace a branch only where the branch
mispredicts on realistic data. A predictable branch is nearly free; a `cmov` on the carried chain is not, because it
turns a control dependency the core would speculate past into a data dependency it must wait for. LLVM turns `cmov`
back into a branch in inner loops when the condition's cost is high relative to the operands' and the mispredict
penalty [LLVM-cmov L10–32]. Decide per branch, from `branch-misses` on real input.
> *Means* — 10.8 [LLVM-cmov]. *Governs* — transformation. *CALM* — not applicable. *Checked by* — `branch-misses` on
> realistic input, kept with the claim. *Brief* — Go branchless only where the branch mispredicts on real data.

**X86.4 Bytes a register or a vector at a time.** Byte-wise work shall not be a byte loop. Compare a vector against a
broadcast, `pmovmskb` to a mask, walk the set bits with `tzcnt` and `x & (x − 1)` [Memchr L1–100]; classify 32 or 64
bytes with `pshufb` as a 16-entry table [SJ-haswell L43–93]; turn a 64-step serial prefix XOR into one carry-less
multiply [SJ-x86-bitmask L18–24]; validate eight ASCII digits in one `uint64_t` loaded by `memcpy`, with the byte order
explicit [FastFloat L142–175]; handle a ragged end with one overlapping unaligned load at each end, which is glibc's
first rule for `memmove` [Glibc-memmove L19–49] and folly's for `memcpy` [Folly-memcpy L16–40]. Divide by a constant
with a multiply and shift, which the compiler does; divide by a run-time invariant with a precomputed reciprocal.
> *Means* — 10.8 [Memchr] [SJ-haswell]. *Governs* — transformation. *CALM* — not applicable. *Checked by* — review; a
> byte loop over a buffer in hot code is a finding. *Brief* — Bytes a register or vector at a time: movemask and
> tzcnt, pshufb tables, overlapping loads for tails; never a byte loop.

**X86.5 Store forwarding, aliasing and false dependencies.** A reload shall have the same width and start address as
the store it follows: forwarding then costs 2 clocks for a general register on Zen 5, and a partly overlapping or wider
read about 12, up to 28 when unaligned [Fog §25.17]; vectors are assembled in registers, not through memory. Streams
shall not sit a multiple of 4 KiB apart, which is why glibc picks its copy direction from the low address bits
[Glibc-memmove]. False dependencies are broken where they arise: 8- and 16-bit destination writes merge with the old
value, `popcnt`, `lzcnt` and `tzcnt` depended on their destination on Intel cores through Skylake, and legacy SSE after
AVX depends on the dirty upper half; `xor dst, dst` first, 32-bit operations, and `vzeroupper` before non-VEX code
[Fog §25.11, §25.14].
> *Means* — 10.8 [Fog §25.17]. *Governs* — transformation. *CALM* — not applicable. *Checked by* — a store-forwarding
> counter beside the claim; review. *Brief* — Reload at the store's width and address; no 4 KiB-spaced streams; break
> false dependencies with `xor` and `vzeroupper`.

**X86.6 Orderings are the language's, not the hardware's.** Every variable shared between threads shall be an atomic
with a stated memory order. On x86 every load, and every relaxed or release store, is a plain `mov`; a seq_cst store is
an `xchg`; acquire and release fences emit nothing [CppMap]. The hardware gives acquire and release for free, so only
the compiler enforces them, and code that has run only on x86 has never had its orderings tested. A full fence is
placed exactly where correctness depends on a store being visible before a later load, the store-buffer pattern, and
nowhere else. It is a locked read-modify-write, not `mfence`: Linux's `smp_mb()` is `lock addl $0,-4(%rsp)`
[Lx-x86-barrier L22–60], adopted for a measured win on virtio [Lx-lockadd]; `mfence` costs 33 to 82 cycles by core
[uops-MFENCE]; GCC 11 and LLVM 21 lower a seq_cst fence the same way [LLVM-lockor]. Non-temporal stores are outside
TSO, so `sfence` goes between them and the store that publishes them [SDM3 §10.2.4] [Glibc-memmove]. Correctness is
shown on the language model, with TSan or Miri [Miri26], and with a litmus test under herd7 for a new protocol, then
on a weak machine (modules AA and RV).
> *Means* — 3.45, 4.6 [TSO] [CppMap]. *Governs* — effect. *CALM* — needs closure: an ordering constraint is
> coordination, spent only where the binding names it. *Checked by* — TSan or Miri in tests; a litmus test for each
> new protocol. *Brief* — Every shared variable an atomic with a stated order; a full fence only at the store→load
> pattern, as a locked RMW; `sfence` after non-temporal stores; test on the language model, never on x86 alone.

**X86.7 Atomicity needs alignment.** Every atomic shall be naturally aligned and never in a packed struct: a locked
operation that crosses a cache line is a split lock [SDM3 §10.1]. Aligned accesses up to 8 bytes are single-copy
atomic; 16-byte aligned SSE and AVX loads and stores are atomic only on processors that enumerate AVX, which the SDM now
guarantees [SDM3 §10.1.1]; a 16-byte atomic rests on that guarantee or on `cmpxchg16b`, which writes and so faults on
read-only memory.
> *Means* — 10.2 [SDM3 §10.1.1]. *Governs* — state. *CALM* — not applicable. *Checked by* — an alignment assertion on
> every atomic's address; `split_lock_detect` on in test runs. *Brief* — Atomics naturally aligned, never packed;
> 16-byte atomics only under the SDM's AVX guarantee.

**X86.8 Floating point reproduces on purpose.** Fused multiply-add contraction shall be decided, not inherited. GCC
contracts `a*b + c` by default outside strict ISO modes [GCC-opt]; baseline `x86-64` has no FMA and `x86-64-v3` does, so
the same source gives `0` at one level and `−2⁻⁶⁰` at the other (measured 2026-09-25 with GCC 13.3 and Clang 18.1 on a
Core Ultra 9 285; `-std=c11` keeps them apart). Where results must reproduce: `-ffp-contract=off` and an explicit
`fma()` where fusion is meant; a fixed reduction order, since vectorising and multiple accumulators reassociate; no
`rcpps` or `rsqrtps`, which are specified by an error bound and so differ by vendor; and MXCSR left alone, because a
shared library built with `-ffast-math` has set flush-to-zero for every program that loaded it.
> *Means* — 3.60, 10.8 [GCC-opt]. *Governs* — transformation. *CALM* — not applicable. *Checked by* — a golden-value
> test built at two `-march` levels. *Brief* — Contraction on or off by decision; results reproduce across `-march`;
> reductions in a fixed order; MXCSR untouched.

**X86.9 The hardware's answer is not the language's.** A shift by the operand width, `INT64_MIN / −1`, an out-of-range
float→int conversion, a misaligned dereference, a racy plain `int`, an overlapping `memcpy`: each has a defined x86
result (the input unchanged, a `#DE` trap, `0x8000…`, it works, TSO-ordered, direction-dependent) and each is undefined
in C, C++ and unsafe Rust, so it passes on x86 and is miscompiled or breaks elsewhere. Scalar `shl` by 64 returns the
input; `psllq` by 64 returns 0 (measured as in X86.8), so scalar and vectorised code disagree. The answer is enforced by
a type or a check, never by what x86 happens to do. A read past a buffer's end is sound only in assembly, within one
page, under a written contract; the better libraries overlap in bounds instead [Memchr L66–77].
> *Means* — 9.1, 10.2 [Miri26]. *Governs* — transformation. *CALM* — not applicable. *Checked by* — UBSan (shift,
> overflow, alignment, float-cast), ASan, Miri. *Brief* — Never rely on x86's answer to undefined behaviour; enforce by
> type or check; over-read only in asm, in-page, under contract.

**X86.10 Hand assembly keeps the ABI.** Assembly shall keep 16-byte stack alignment at each call, the direction flag
clear, the callee-saved registers, and shall assume no red zone where a signal or interrupt can land, as zstd's decoder
states in its header [Zstd-huf L51–60]; it carries `endbr64`, CFI directives and a GNU-stack note; it exists only for a
measured gain and behind a C fallback whose tests run against it.
> *Means* — 10.7, 10.8 [Zstd-huf]. *Governs* — transformation. *CALM* — not applicable. *Checked by* — the fallback's
> tests run against the assembly (3.58). *Brief* — Hand asm keeps the ABI, carries `endbr64` and CFI, is justified by
> a measurement and fenced by a fallback.

**X86.11 Measure as the experts do.** A performance claim shall name the core, its microcode revision, the compiler and
its flags; be counted in cycles per element on a pinned core over varied, realistic input; report minimum and median
with the run count; show the counter that says why (top-down: `perf stat -M TopdownL1` on Intel, `PipelineL1` on Zen 4
and 5); and be re-run on the other vendor and after microcode updates, which have removed fast paths before
[Downs-zero]. Predict first from uops.info and a speed-limit estimate [Downs-limits]; vary the input, because branch
predictors memorise repeated data; read the generated assembly. Contention has its own price list, from a cache-line
migration to a system call to a context switch [Downs-costs].
> *Means* — 10.8 [Downs-limits]. *Governs* — effect. *CALM* — not applicable. *Checked by* — a measurement record with
> those fields beside the claim. *Brief* — Claims name core, microcode, compiler and flags; cycles per element; min and
> median; the counter that explains it; both vendors, again after microcode.

**X86.12 Silicon lies at scale.** Where results matter across a fleet, computed data shall be checked end to end:
individual cores compute wrong answers on particular instructions and pass manufacturing test [Hochschild21 p.1]
[Dixit21 p.1]. Hardware random numbers are mixed through the operating system's generator, because `RDRAND` and
`RDSEED` have returned constants with the carry flag set. A fast path that is undocumented is temporary: zero-store
and move elimination were switched off by microcode, gathers were slowed for a side channel [Downs-zero] [Zenbleed].
> *Means* — 4.8, 5.5 [Hochschild21]. *Governs* — effect. *CALM* — not applicable. *Checked by* — end-to-end checksums
> in the design; review. *Brief* — At scale, checksum computed data end to end; hardware entropy only through the OS
> generator; an undocumented fast path is temporary.

## The price list

Core clocks, read in September 2026; each row names its machine and source.

| Operation | Cost | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Simple integer op | 1 clock, up to 6 per clock on Zen 5 | [Fog §25.8] |
| Register `mov`, zero idiom | 0 when elimination is on; Ice Lake microcode turned GPR move elimination off | [Fog §25.13] [Downs-zero] |
| Vector integer op, Zen 5 | 2 clocks effective, all widths; vector moves 0 | [Fog §25.9] |
| FP add, multiply, FMA, Zen 5 | 2, 3, 4 clocks; two FMA per clock | [Fog §25.9] |
| L1D, L2 hit, Zen 5 | 4, 14 clocks | [Fog §25.16] |
| Store→load forward, Zen 5 | 2 clocks GPR, 9 vector to 256 bits, 11 at 512; 0 with memory-operand mirroring | [Fog §25.17–25.18] |
| Store-forward failure, Zen 5 | ~12 clocks; up to 28 unaligned | [Fog §25.17] |
| 64-bit `div` | tens of clocks on Skylake; 14 on Ice Lake and after | [uops-DIV] |
| `lock add [m], r`, uncontended | ~18 clocks Intel through Alder Lake; 7 to 20 on Zen 3 to 5 | [uops-LOCKADD] |
| `mfence` | 33 to 38 Intel; 58 to 82 Zen 2 to 5 | [uops-MFENCE] |
| `pdep`, `pext` | 1 µop Intel and Zen 3+; ~18 clocks throughput Zen 1 and 2 | [uops-PDEP] |
| `vpcompressd` to memory | 72 clocks Zen 4; 3 Zen 5; 2 Intel | [uops-VPCOMPRESSD] |
| Subnormal operand or result | a few clocks on Zen; on the order of 100 on Intel cores without FTZ/DAZ | [Fog §25.10] |
| Contended line, system call, context switch | ~40–400 ns, ~1 µs, ~10 µs (Skylake) | [Downs-costs] |

## Traps

| Trap | What happens | What the best code does |
|---|---|---|
| Store-forward failure | narrow stores then a wide reload; vector↔scalar through memory | same width and address; build in registers (X86.5) |
| 4 KiB aliasing | a load matching an older store's address modulo 4 KiB is held | choose direction and offsets by the low address bits [Glibc-memmove] |
| Vendor-specific slow instructions | `pdep` on Zen 2, `vpcompressd` to memory on Zen 4, `bt m, r` | uops.info for every target; compress to a register then store |
| Front-end cliffs | jumps on 32-byte boundaries on Skylake-derived cores after the JCC microcode; length-changing prefixes | the assembler's boundary alignment where the fleet needs it |
| Microcode reprices | elimination fast paths and gathers slowed in the field | re-baseline after updates; build on documented behaviour [Downs-zero] |
| AVX-512 licences | Skylake-SP downclocks under 512-bit work; Ice Lake client ~100 MHz; Zen 5 none | matters on older Intel fleets only; measure there |
| Split locks | a locked op across two lines; the kernel warns, throttles or kills | align every atomic (X86.7) |

## Exemplars

- simdjson, `src/haswell.cpp` [SJ-haswell L43–93]: a nibble-table classifier whose comment states its known false
  positives and where they are caught; `bitmask.h` [SJ-x86-bitmask L18–24]: a serial scan as one `pclmulqdq`.
- memchr, `arch/generic/memchr.rs` [Memchr L1–100]: one algorithm over a vector trait for SSE2, AVX2, NEON and wasm, the
  design written as prose in the file, in-bounds overlap instead of over-read.
- BLAKE3, `c/blake3_dispatch.c` [B3-dispatch L108–165]: CPUID and XGETBV done right, and a comment anticipating the
  data race TSan will report on the cached feature word.
- zstd, `huf_decompress_amd64.S` [Zstd-huf L51–100]: hand assembly with a documented register map, bounds hoisted,
  the ABI stated, and a C fallback.
- glibc, `memmove-vec-unaligned-erms.S` [Glibc-memmove L19–49]: the algorithm as a numbered specification at the top of
  the file; one source for SSE2, AVX2 and EVEX; aliasing-aware direction; `sfence` after non-temporal stores.
- Linux, `arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S` [Lx-x86-memcpy L13–60]: patched at boot to a bare `rep movsb` on cores with fast
  short `rep movsb`; `arch/x86/include/asm/barrier.h` [Lx-x86-barrier L22–60]: the cheapest correct full barrier,
  compiler-only read and write barriers because TSO already orders them, and a `cmp; sbb` index mask.
- folly, `memcpy.S` [Folly-memcpy L16–40]: a `memcpy` made safe for overlap because programs relied on it after glibc's
  backward copy broke them.
- fast_float, `ascii_number.h` [FastFloat L142–175]: SWAR with loads that are not undefined behaviour and an explicit
  byte order.

## Forward look, to about 2031

- APX: 32 general registers, three-operand integer ops, a no-flags form, conditional loads, stores and compares
  [APX]; Nova Lake is the first client part expected to ship it. Register pressure stops being an x86 tax; dispatch
  stays mandatory because older cores cannot run the encoding.
- AVX10 versions the AVX-512 feature set and makes 512 bits universal on new Intel cores; dispatch tests the version.
  Zen 6 adds FP16 and further AVX-512 subsets per AMD's own toolchain patches. The 2021 to 2026 Intel client base
  without AVX-512 keeps dispatch necessary through the decade.
- Memory keeps getting relatively dearer: Yee measured that one Zen 5 core needs on the order of 340 AVX-512
  instructions per 512-bit load to avoid saturating bandwidth [Yee24]; layout and memory-level parallelism gain value
  over instruction tricks.
- Security keeps repricing fast paths, and memory tagging is coming to the ISA through the vendors' advisory group;
  treat pointer representation and allocators as the places that will change.

## Questions an expert asks of x86-64 code before calling it done

1. What is the baseline level, what is dispatched above it, and does dispatch check XGETBV as well as CPUID?
2. Has it run on Intel and AMD, including the oldest supported core, with each hot instruction checked on uops.info?
3. What is the predicted bottleneck, and do the top-down counters agree?
4. What is the loop-carried chain, and is its latency covered by independent accumulators, streams or lanes?
5. Is each branchless construct on the critical path truly unpredictable on realistic data?
6. Any store→load width or offset mismatches, 4 KiB-spaced streams, partial-register writes, SSE after AVX without
   `vzeroupper`?
7. Is every shared variable an atomic with a stated order, and is it correct under TSan, Miri or herd7, not merely on
   x86?
8. Where does correctness depend on store→load ordering, and is there a full fence exactly there?
9. Are all atomics naturally aligned, and is any 16-byte atomic backed by the documented guarantee?
10. Is there an `sfence` between non-temporal stores and the store that publishes them?
11. Is contraction deliberately on or off, and does output change between `-march=x86-64` and `x86-64-v3`?
12. Is MXCSR changed anywhere, including by a dependency, and restored?
13. Can a shift reach the operand width, a division be `MIN / −1`, a conversion overflow, a pointer be misaligned, with
    the answer enforced by type or check?
14. Does anything read past a buffer's end, and if so only in assembly, within a page, under a written contract?
15. Does hand assembly keep the ABI: stack alignment, DF clear, callee-saved registers, no red zone where signals land,
    `endbr64`, CFI?
16. Was the claim measured in cycles on a pinned core, recording CPU, microcode, compiler and flags, over varied
    input, with minimum and median and the assembly read?
17. Would a microcode or kernel update that removes a fast path change the conclusion, and would a benchmark notice?

<!-- brief: x86-64 -->
Reason from the model, confirm on each vendor: name the baseline level and dispatch above it; write hot loops against
the carried chain; branchless only where the branch mispredicts; bytes a vector at a time; reload at the store's
width; every shared variable an atomic with a stated order and a locked RMW where a full fence is needed, tested on
the language model not on x86; atomics aligned; contraction by decision; never rely on x86's answer to undefined
behaviour; claims name core, microcode, compiler and flags, in cycles, with the counter that explains them.
